notes.text:
# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; prediction before batch 1]
Under a common charge (0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.080 L reaction solvent), catalyst identity and thermal exposure will dominate conversion/selectivity. I will screen categorical catalysts and temperatures rather than infer ordering from indices. A post-reaction HPLC measurement should distinguish low conversion from purification loss.

## H2 [tentative; prediction before batch 1]
The nominal dossier suggests X0 has the largest product organic fraction and selectivity at its stated contact conditions. A single extraction into X0 followed by retaining the organic phase should improve purity but cap recovery near the extracted product fraction; larger organic/aqueous ratio and an organic wash may change that tradeoff. This prior could be misindexed and will be tested against assays.

Decision rule: prioritize completed processes with measured purity >=0.80, then maximize measured recovery; replicate the most promising region if campaign capacity permits. Numerical differences smaller than stated instrumental/process uncertainty will be treated as unresolved.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [supported only within S0, 390 K, 7200 s]
Catalyst identity strongly changes the reaction mixture. Post-reaction HPLC gave approximate yield/selectivity: C0 0.184/0.344 (event 0041), C1 0.254/0.493 (0057), C2 0.136/0.237 (0073), C3 0.299/0.580 (0089). Differences are much larger than the declared HPLC standard deviations, though each condition is unreplicated. C3 is the provisional reaction catalyst; C1 remains a plausible alternative if downstream purity dominates.

## H2 [unresolved / narrowed]
X0 extraction plus one 0.040 L wash did not reach purity 0.80 in the S0 catalyst screen: final purities ranged about 0.407–0.712 (events 0052, 0068, 0084, 0100), with low recoveries. The nominal X0 selectivity prior is therefore insufficient for these reaction mixtures. Reaction-solvent screening is now preferred over assuming more washing alone will solve selectivity.

## H3 [procedural confound identified]
Concentrate requires an established phase system. Batch 2 attempted concentration before adding aqueous phase and then selected a nonexistent organic phase, losing the reaction material (events 0024–0029); its final assay is not evidence about chemistry. Correct workup order is quench, add aqueous phase, concentrate, add extractant, mix/settle, retain organic, wash/dry.

Next test: hold C3/390 K/7200 s and screen S1–S3. If a solvent materially raises post-reaction selectivity and final purity, optimize that solvent; otherwise compare C1 under the best solvent or add a second wash.

# Campaign hypotheses — final source-stage record

## H1 [supported within tested grid]
Reaction-solvent identity materially affected the C3/390 K/7200 s mixture. Relative to S0 (HPLC yield/selectivity 0.299/0.580, event 0089), S1 raised yield to 0.415 but selectivity was 0.537 (0105), S2 gave the best tested yield at 0.460 with selectivity 0.574 (0121), and S3 was poor at 0.199/0.236 (0137). S2/C3 is therefore the best tested reaction region, though repeats show process variation (events 0153 and 0170).

## H2 [rejected as a route to the 0.80 constraint in this campaign]
Neither switching from X0 to X1 with two washes nor lowering temperature to 370 K with two X0 washes produced purity >=0.80: final purities were 0.638 (event 0165) and 0.679 (0182). The small-volume X0 extraction prediction also failed sharply (purity 0.467, event 0198), so the nominal partition anchors are not reliable enough outside their stated contact scope and cannot justify extrapolated purity.

## H3 [decision]
No completed assay reached purity 0.80. Batch 8 is the best compromise among observed completed materials: S2/C3 at 390 K for 7200 s, X0 workup with one wash gave purity 0.719 and recovery 0.150 (event 0132), both better jointly than alternatives near it. Batch 1 had slightly higher purity (~0.734, event 0017) but zero measured recovery and a confounded doubled charge. I will recommend batch 8 while explicitly noting that it misses the purity specification; a future study should investigate a different orthogonal purification rather than infer that extra washing or lower extractant volume will succeed.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

1. Scope and interpretation

This is an anonymous synthetic reaction-to-purification world. Catalyst, solvent, and extractant indices are categorical labels, not chemical identities. My model therefore concerns operational relationships among charge, catalyst, solvent, thermal exposure, reaction composition, phase partitioning, washing, and final recovery. It should not be interpreted as a molecular mechanism for real substances.

The campaign contained 12 completed batches. The most reliable reaction evidence came from pre-workup HPLC measurements, while the final assays were authoritative for the actual objectives of final purity and recovery. These two measurements sampled different process states. In particular, final-assay conversion was often near 1 because the selected organic product phase contained little residual reactant; it should not be read as evidence that the reactor itself achieved nearly complete conversion. The pre-workup HPLC conversion is the better reaction-progress indicator.

2. Proposed reaction model

A useful phenomenological scheme is

reactant -> target product
reactant -> byproducts/degradation products,

with catalyst and reaction solvent changing the relative effective rates. A minimal kinetic representation would be

dR/dt = -(k_target + k_side) R,
dP/dt = k_target R - k_loss P,
dI/dt = k_side R + k_loss P,

where each rate constant depends on catalyst c, solvent s, and temperature T. For example, k_j(c,s,T) could follow an Arrhenius-like form A_j(c,s) exp[-E_j(c,s)/(RT)]. The data do not identify these parameters separately; they only show their combined effects at a few times and temperatures.

At the measurement level, reaction yield was approximately governed by conversion times selectivity,

Y_reaction approximately X x S,

subject to independent measurement noise and process-state definitions. For example, batch 8 had HPLC conversion 0.760, selectivity 0.574, and yield 0.460; 0.760 x 0.574 is close to, although not exactly, the observed yield. The mismatch is consistent with separately calibrated noisy channels and possibly different normalization details.

3. Thermal exposure

Within the unconfounded C0/S0 series, increasing thermal exposure strongly increased conversion and yield. Batch 2 at 330 K for 1800 s gave HPLC conversion 0.0724, yield 0.0232, and selectivity 0.3168. Batch 3 at 390 K for 7200 s gave conversion 0.5507, yield 0.1845, and selectivity 0.3437. Thus the primary effect of greater temperature/time exposure was faster reaction, with only a modest selectivity change for C0.

Batch 1, at 350 K for 3600 s, gave HPLC conversion 0.2031 and yield 0.0687, broadly consistent with this trend, but it is chemically confounded: both an ordinary reagent charge and component 0 were added, consuming twice the intended reagent stock. Its results cannot isolate temperature or time.

The temperature comparison for the preferred C3/S2 region was less decisive. Batch 8 at 390 K for 7200 s gave HPLC conversion 0.760, yield 0.460, and selectivity 0.574. Batch 11 at 370 K for 7200 s gave conversion 0.655, yield 0.413, and selectivity 0.557. This supports the conjecture that 390 K accelerated conversion without a large selectivity penalty over this range. Because each temperature had only one relevant batch and their workups differed, a detailed activation law is not identifiable.

4. Catalyst effects

Batches 3-6 screened all four catalysts under S0 at 390 K for 7200 s with otherwise comparable charges. Their pre-workup HPLC yield/selectivity values were:

- Batch 3, C0: yield 0.184, selectivity 0.344, conversion 0.551.
- Batch 4, C1: yield 0.254, selectivity 0.493, conversion 0.525.
- Batch 5, C2: yield 0.136, selectivity 0.237, conversion 0.631.
- Batch 6, C3: yield 0.299, selectivity 0.580, conversion 0.527.

These large differences, relative to the declared HPLC uncertainties, show that the catalysts mainly altered branching between productive and side pathways rather than simply ranking by conversion. C2 produced the highest conversion in this screen but the lowest useful selectivity and a poor yield. C3 produced only moderate conversion but the best selectivity and yield. C1 was intermediate and remained a plausible alternative where downstream purity was emphasized. Thus catalyst activity and catalyst selectivity are distinct latent variables in this world.

5. Reaction-solvent effects and catalyst-solvent coupling

Batches 6-9 held C3, 390 K, and 7200 s approximately fixed while screening solvents. The HPLC results were:

- Batch 6, S0: conversion 0.527, yield 0.299, selectivity 0.580, purity 0.563.
- Batch 7, S1: conversion 0.795, yield 0.415, selectivity 0.537, purity 0.561.
- Batch 8, S2: conversion 0.760, yield 0.460, selectivity 0.574, purity 0.624.
- Batch 9, S3: conversion 0.736, yield 0.199, selectivity 0.236, purity 0.304.

Solvent therefore affected both reaction rate and pathway branching. S1 and S2 substantially increased conversion relative to S0. S2 retained good selectivity and gave the best tested reaction yield and reaction-mixture purity. S3 achieved substantial conversion but diverted material strongly into byproducts. A separable model such as k(c,T) multiplied by a solvent-only factor may be too simple: the observations are more naturally described by catalyst-solvent-specific productive and side-reaction coefficients, although only C3 received a complete solvent screen, so the interaction cannot be estimated generally.

Batches 8 and 10 provide a partial repeat of the C3/S2/390 K/7200 s reaction before different workups. Batch 8 measured conversion 0.760, yield 0.460, selectivity 0.574, and purity 0.624. Batch 10 measured 0.792, 0.425, 0.565, and 0.627. Their close selectivity and purity support the robustness of the qualitative S2 conclusion, while the conversion and yield differences reveal non-negligible process variation beyond nominal instrument noise.

6. Extraction and purification model

The nominal dossier suggested an equilibrium partition model. If K_p and K_i are product and impurity distribution coefficients and V_o/V_a is the organic-to-aqueous volume ratio, an ideal single-contact organic recovery fraction would be

f_j = K_j V_o / (V_a + K_j V_o),

and the extractive enrichment would be related to K_p/K_i. The dossier ranked X0 highly, with nominal K_product 2.585, K_impurity 0.552, and selectivity ratio about 4.69 at a specific 298.15 K, 240 s, 0.018 L organic/0.030 L aqueous contact. X1 had lower nominal coefficients and a similar nominal selectivity ratio.

The operational data support only the broad idea of differential partitioning, not quantitative transfer of those coefficients. The successful workup order was: quench; add an aqueous phase; concentrate the phase system to create vessel capacity; add extractant; mix; settle; retain the organic phase; wash; dry; terminate; assay. Batch 2 demonstrated an important bookkeeping/process constraint: concentration before establishing a phase system failed, X0 could not then be added at the requested volume, and selection of a nonexistent organic phase removed the reaction material. Its final blank-like assay is not chemical evidence.

For comparable C3/S2 feeds, batch 8 used X0 and one wash, producing final purity 0.7187 and recovery 0.1501. Batch 10 used X1 and two washes, producing purity 0.6377 and recovery 0.1008, despite very similar pre-workup HPLC purities of 0.624 and 0.627. This changed my initial explanation: the nominal dossier did not make X1 a superior high-purity option in the actual process, and X0 was empirically better in this scope.

Additional washing was not monotonically beneficial. Batch 11 used X0 with two washes and ended at purity 0.6788 and recovery 0.0829. Its feed and temperature were not exactly identical to batch 8, so this is not a clean one-factor comparison, but it gives no evidence that a second wash solved the purity problem. It is plausible that washing removed some product as well as impurity, or that phase entrainment and stochastic process variation dominated the small expected enrichment.

I also conjectured from the equilibrium equation that decreasing X0 volume would sacrifice recovery but improve purity by approaching the limiting K_product/K_impurity enrichment. Batch 12 tested a 0.010 L X0 contact after the preferred C3/S2 reaction and contradicted that extrapolation: final purity was only 0.4675 and recovery 0.0473. Possible explanations include insufficient extractive capacity, incomplete transfer, phase-handling losses, or a dossier that is misindexed or valid only near its stated contact conditions. The data do not distinguish these alternatives. The failed prediction is strong evidence against using the simple equilibrium formula quantitatively outside the dossier scope.

Drying and concentration chiefly changed volume and handling state. There was no direct evidence that they generated target product. Their likely roles were removal of water or volatile carrier and provision of vessel capacity, with potential small loss or degradation. No experiment independently varied drying, so its chemical effect is unidentifiable.

7. Relationship between reaction quality and final performance

Good reaction selectivity was necessary but not sufficient for final purity and recovery. Across the C0-C3 S0 screen, final purity/recovery values were approximately:

- Batch 3, C0: 0.561/0.0345.
- Batch 4, C1: 0.712/0.0422.
- Batch 5, C2: 0.407/0.0182.
- Batch 6, C3: 0.666/0.0458.

This broadly follows the pre-workup selectivity ranking, showing that byproducts created in the reactor propagated into the workup. However, the preferred S2 solvent increased the amount of target available for extraction: batch 8 reached final recovery 0.150, much higher than the S0 batches. The workup then imposed a substantial recovery penalty; batch 8 had pre-workup HPLC recovery 0.458 but final recovery 0.150.

The final-assay conversion values near 0.98-1.00 in many batches should not override this interpretation. Phase selection removed most unreacted reagent with the discarded aqueous material, causing the retained organic sample to appear nearly free of reactant. Similarly, final-assay selectivity channels used a downstream sample context and were not interchangeable with reactor HPLC selectivity. Final purity and recovery are the meaningful downstream variables.

Final process mass-balance errors were generally small, around zero to roughly 0.0065 in the cited successful batches, comparable to the declared assay uncertainty. This suggests the low recoveries were mainly modeled separation losses rather than gross numerical mass-balance failures, although the assay cannot reveal exactly where product was lost.

8. Experiments that changed the explanation

Batch 2 established that phase existence and operation order are mechanistically important; it forced correction of the workup sequence.

Batches 3-6 separated catalyst activity from selectivity and identified C3 as the best productive catalyst in S0, overturning any assumption that maximum conversion alone was desirable.

Batches 6-9 revealed the major solvent coupling. Batch 8 made S2 the preferred reaction solvent, whereas batch 9 showed that high conversion in S3 could coexist with severe side-product formation.

Batch 10 contradicted the idea that X1 plus additional washing would improve final purity. Batch 11 weakened the idea that more washing was monotonically beneficial. Batch 12 directly contradicted the quantitative extrapolation that a smaller X0 phase would necessarily increase purity.

9. Limits and unidentifiable factors

No batch achieved the required final purity of 0.80. The highest observed purity was about 0.734 in batch 1, but its recovery was reported as zero and its doubled charge was confounded. The strongest joint outcome was batch 8 at purity 0.7187 and recovery 0.1501; it was selected as the least-bad observed compromise, not as a specification-compliant process.

The campaign cannot identify molecular structures, elementary reaction steps, activation energies, true rate constants, phase compositions, or wash-solvent identity. Catalyst-solvent interactions outside C3 were not mapped. Temperature and residence time were mostly changed together, preventing their independent estimation. Most conditions were unreplicated, and batches 8 and 10 were only partial reaction repeats followed by different workups. The effects of atmosphere, pressure, feedback control, mixing speed, settling time, wash number, drying, and concentration duration were not independently screened. The role of component 0 is also unidentifiable because it appeared only in the confounded first batch.

Plausible alternative explanations include hidden catalyst deactivation, solvent-dependent analytical response within the synthetic calibration, kinetic rather than equilibrium extraction, phase entrainment, nonlinear capacity limits, and a deliberately misindexed nominal dossier. These alternatives fit parts of the evidence and cannot be resolved from this campaign.

10. Overall working mechanism

My final working account is a coupled network rather than a single optimum law:

1. Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time determine conversion and competitive target/side-product formation.
2. C3 strongly favors the target relative to the other catalysts tested, while S2 provides the best observed balance of conversion and selectivity with C3.
3. Quenching stops or greatly slows reaction chemistry and establishes a workable downstream state.
4. Aqueous addition and controlled concentration create a two-phase feed and sufficient vessel capacity.
5. Extractant identity and phase ratio govern incomplete, competitive transfer of target and impurity, but the nominal equilibrium coefficients are only local priors.
6. Washing and drying can remove impurities and carrier liquid but also incur product loss; more washing is not guaranteed to increase purity.
7. Selecting only the organic phase can make downstream conversion appear nearly complete while overall recovery remains low.

Within the tested scope, the best-supported process region is C3/S2 at about 390 K for 7200 s followed by the corrected X0 single-contact, single-wash workup. Its observed batch-8 result is real campaign evidence, but extrapolation beyond that recipe—or a claim that it meets purity 0.80—is not supported.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign because they use only 0.00025 mol C1 catalyst, solvent volume 0.028 L, and X2 extractant; the campaign used 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.080 L solvent, and mainly X0. I therefore used broad predictive intervals that include process uncertainty as well as final-assay noise. For the 0.040 mol feeds, catalyst loading is only 0.625 mol%, about twentyfold below the campaign loading. I predict low conversion and very low recovery, with 7200 s improving recovery over 1800 s but allowing somewhat more side-product formation. X0 is predicted to outperform X2 modestly, consistent with its higher nominal product partition coefficient and selectivity. With X2, a smaller organic phase should enrich the product but reduce recovery, while a larger phase should do the reverse. For the 0.002 mol feeds, catalyst loading is 12.5 mol%, close to the campaign regime, so substantially greater fractional conversion and recovery are expected despite the dilute feed. Washing is predicted to raise purity while losing some target; two staged washes should be slightly more selective than one equal-total-volume wash, although campaign batches 8, 10, and 11 showed that washing effects were variable and not reliably monotonic. Post-workup concentration is predicted to have little compositional benefit and a small possible degradation or handling loss. HPLC sampling, drying, the 0.97 transfer, and final-assay sampling are included as small recovery losses. The intervals are especially wide because catalyst-loading response, C1–S2 coupling, X2 behavior, and low-charge kinetics were not directly identified.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific mechanism or optimum was supplied. The only substantive prior was the nominal extraction dossier, explicitly qualified as incomplete and possibly misindexed.

Supported within the tested scope:
- Greater thermal exposure increased reaction progress. C0/S0 gave HPLC conversion 0.072 in batch 2 at 330 K for 1800 s versus 0.551 in batch 3 at 390 K for 7200 s. Temperature and time were changed together, so their separate effects remain unidentified.
- Catalyst identity controlled pathway branching, not merely conversion. Under the common S0/390 K/7200 s screen, C3 in batch 6 gave the highest HPLC yield/selectivity (0.299/0.580), while C2 in batch 5 gave higher conversion (0.631) but poor yield/selectivity (0.136/0.237).
- Reaction solvent strongly coupled to productive and side pathways. With C3, S2 in batch 8 gave the best HPLC yield, 0.460, whereas S3 in batch 9 gave substantial conversion, 0.736, but only 0.199 yield and 0.236 selectivity.
- The approximate empirical law yield ≈ conversion × selectivity was useful but not exact. Batch 8, for example, had conversion 0.760, selectivity 0.574, and measured yield 0.460.
- Phase-operation order mattered. Batch 2 showed that concentration before establishing a phase system failed; subsequent selection of a nonexistent organic phase lost the reaction material.

Partly supported:
- The dossier’s qualitative preference for X0 over weaker alternatives received some support. Similar C3/S2 feeds gave final purity/recovery 0.719/0.150 with X0 and one wash in batch 8, versus 0.638/0.101 with X1 and two washes in batch 10. This was not a clean single-factor comparison because wash staging also differed.
- C3/S2 was repeatably promising: batches 8 and 10 had similar pre-workup selectivity and purity, although their conversion and yield differed enough to indicate process variability.

Contradicted or substantially weakened:
- Quantitative extrapolation of the dossier’s equilibrium partition coefficients was contradicted. I expected a smaller X0 phase to trade recovery for higher purity, but batch 12 produced only 0.467 purity and 0.047 recovery.
- The conjecture that more washing would monotonically improve purity was weakened. Batch 11 used two X0 washes but gave 0.679 purity and 0.083 recovery, worse jointly than batch 8’s one-wash result. Temperature also differed, so this is not definitive proof of a negative wash effect.
- High downstream conversion was not evidence of high reactor conversion. Final assays often reported conversion near one after phase disposal even when pre-workup HPLC conversion was much lower. This changed my interpretation of the final-assay conversion channel.

Untested or unresolved:
- Independent temperature and residence-time laws, catalyst-order kinetics, catalyst deactivation, atmosphere and pressure effects, and general catalyst–solvent interactions were not identified.
- X2 and X3 extractants were not actually tested during the campaign, despite appearing in the nominal dossier.
- The isolated effects of drying, post-selection concentration, wash staging, mixing speed, and settling time remain untested.
- The role of component 0 is unresolved because it appeared only in confounded batch 1.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would perform a within-vessel catalyst-step experiment under the extrapolative regime used in the prediction questions: 0.040 mol reagent in 0.028 L S2 with C1 at 400 K. Start with 0.00025 mol catalyst, heat for 3600 s, and take an HPLC measurement. Then add 0.00475 mol more C1, heat for another 3600 s at the same temperature, and take a second HPLC measurement before carrying out a fixed workup.

The leading explanation is that the very low catalyst-to-reagent ratio makes the high-charge prediction recipes catalyst-limited. The main alternative is that conversion is governed primarily by thermal or solvent-controlled background kinetics, substrate concentration, or saturation, so increasing catalyst twentyfold would have little immediate effect.

A large post-addition acceleration—such as a substantial conversion and target-yield increase beyond that expected from another equal time interval—would support catalyst limitation and make my very low recovery predictions for Q01-Q06 more credible. Little or no acceleration, with conversion progressing at approximately the original rate, would favor the background-kinetic or saturation alternative and imply that those recovery predictions are too low. A conversion increase accompanied mainly by byproduct growth would support catalyst dependence but require revising the model so that high C1 loading accelerates side pathways as well as target formation. An intermediate result would leave catalyst order unresolved and motivate a true replicated loading series.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and goal effects

Unused evidence included the raw spectral artifacts and most non-objective final-assay channels. No GC, UV-visible, IR, MS, or NMR measurements were used. Atmosphere, pressure, automated control, mixing-speed variation, settling-time variation, and container-transfer strategies were not explored. The nominal X2 and X3 dossier entries were unused experimentally. Batch 1 was largely unusable for causal inference because of its doubled charge, and batch 2 was unusable as a purification result because of the failed workup sequence.

The least reliable predictions are Q01-Q06 because they extrapolate simultaneously to a twentyfold lower catalyst loading, a smaller solvent volume, higher reagent concentration, C1/S2 coupling not observed directly, and mostly untested X2 extraction. Q07-Q12 are also uncertain because they extrapolate to only 0.002 mol reagent and depend on unmeasured low-charge kinetics. Within that set, the staged-wash contrast Q09-Q10 and concentration contrast Q11-Q12 are especially weak because those isolated operation effects were never measured. Their paired directional differences are more defensible than their absolute point estimates.

The batch-8 recommendation is reliable only as a ranking among the completed observations. It is not reliable as a specification-compliant recommendation: its measured purity was 0.719, below the required 0.80.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because the objective required a complete reaction, extraction, and purification process with final purity and recovery, I spent every batch on a completed workup and used the limited extra measurements mainly for one pre-workup HPLC snapshot per batch. That strategy generated relevant end-to-end evidence but left few resources for replication, time courses, catalyst-loading studies, or isolated unit-operation controls. Once no process approached purity 0.80, later batches emphasized alternative extraction and washing choices. This was appropriate for the operational goal but weakened mechanistic identification. I see no evidence of a direct conflict between the goal and honest reporting; the main tradeoff was breadth of process search versus precision of causal inference.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 8 gave the strongest observed joint outcome among completed batches: final-assay purity 0.7187 and recovery 0.1501 (event runner-operation-0132) after the best tested reaction mixture (C3/S2, 390 K, 7200 s) and X0 extraction with one wash. No batch met the required purity >=0.80; this selection is therefore the least-bad evidence-based compromise rather than a claim of specification compliance. Batch 1 had slightly higher purity but zero measured recovery and a confounded doubled charge.
